My office is partnering with the Northampton County Area Agency on Aging to help you apply for the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program at various times throughout the month of July. Eligible seniors may receive vouchers for fresh produce.
Join us to confirm your eligibility and submit your application on:
July 8th from 9:00 AM to 10:30 AM at the Hanover Township (Northampton County) Community Center
OR
July 21st from 9:00 AM to 10:30 AM at the Northampton Borough Recreation Center
July 21st from 2:00 PM to 3:00 PM at the Bath Borough Municipal Building
For more information, please contact my district office at 610-821-8468 or visit my website at
PASenatorMiller.com
.
I look forward to seeing you there!

ai_summary.summary: Senator Nick Miller's office is hosting three in-person events in July 2026, partnering with the Northampton County Area Agency on Aging, to help eligible seniors apply for the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program. The program provides vouchers that seniors can use to purchase fresh produce at farmers markets. Events are scheduled at community centers and municipal buildings in Hanover Township, Northampton Borough, and Bath Borough.

Keeping You Safe from Scams
Scammers are using increasingly sophisticated tactics to try to access people’s personal information. Staying alert is one of the best ways to protect yourself and your loved ones from harm.

MyChart
, the online patient portal used by hospitals and health providers, including St. Luke’s University Health Network and Lehigh Valley Health Network. Pressure to act immediately:
Claims that your account will be closed, a warrant has been issued, or a loved one is in danger to push you into quick decisions.
Unusual payment methods:
Requests for payment through gift cards, cryptocurrency, wire transfers, or payment apps.
Requests for sensitive information:
Asking for passwords, PINs, Social Security numbers, or bank details through phone, text, or email.
Unsolicited contact:
Unexpected calls, emails, or messages from unfamiliar or suspicious sources.
“Too good to be true” offers:
Promises of large sums of money, prizes, or high-return investments with little to no effort.
Suspicious links or attachments:
Messages directing you to fake login pages or containing malware-laden files.
Demand for secrecy:
Instructions not to speak with your bank, family members, or law enforcement about the interaction.

AI Consumer Protection Bill Establishing Advertising Disclosure Standards Heads to Governor
October 8, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA
–
October 8, 2026
– Senators Nick Pisciottano (D-Allegheny), Nick Miller (D-Lehigh/Northampton), who serves as the Democratic Chair of the Senate Communications and Technology Committee, and John Kane (D-Chester/Delaware) are advancing legislation to the Governor’s desk to establish Pennsylvania’s first advertising disclosure standards for AI-generated and significantly AI‑modified content used to market consumer goods and services.
The General Assembly gave final approval to
Senate Bill 806
, sending the consumer protection measure to Gov. Josh Shapiro for his consideration. The legislation would require advertisers to clearly disclose when AI-generated or significantly AI-modified images, audio, video or text are used in advertising in a way that could mislead consumers about a product or service.
“Consumers should know when what they are seeing or hearing in an advertisement was created or significantly altered by artificial intelligence,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “As AI becomes more common in advertising, we need clear standards that protect consumers from all ages from being misled while allowing businesses to responsibly use this technology. Establishing a clear disclosure requirement is an important step toward transparency and accountability in the rapidly evolving world of AI.”
“This is a major step for consumer protection in Pennsylvania,” said
Senator Pisciottano
. “Consumers deserve to know if AI is being used to create a false impression about a product or service. This legislation sets a commonsense transparency standard so Pennsylvanians can make informed decisions about what they are buying, while still allowing businesses to take advantage of this technology.”
“Our ability to trust what we see and hear is being pushed to its limits as AI evolves faster than our ability to verify what’s real,” said
Senator John I. Kane
. “Folks deserve to know the plain truth about the products they’re buying, the images they’re seeing, and the voices they hear online. Transparency isn’t optional in a healthy society; it’s a necessity. By requiring clear disclosure, we’re taking an important step to make sure Pennsylvanians aren’t left exposed when interacting with powerful technology.”
Senate Bill 806 would require an AI disclosure to be clear, conspicuous and presented in the same medium as the AI-generated or modified content. For example, if an advertiser uses an AI-generated image that could cause consumers to believe they are seeing an actual product, the advertisement would be required to disclose that AI was used to create or modify the image.
###

October 7, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA
–
October 7, 2026
− Two transportation priorities advocated by State Sen. Nick Miller (D-Lehigh/Northampton) advanced as the Senate Transportation Committee voted on legislation addressing local RADAR enforcement and modernizing how Pennsylvania drivers can present vehicle registration.
The committee advanced
Senate Bill 509
, sponsored by Sen. Greg Rothman, with an amendment offered by Miller, as well as
Senate Bill 895
, sponsored by Miller.
SB 509 would give municipalities the option to adopt ordinances allowing their local police departments to use RADAR for speed enforcement. The legislation does not require municipalities to adopt the technology and includes provisions prohibiting speed-enforcement quotas and the use of RADAR primarily for generating revenue.
Miller’s SB 895 would allow Pennsylvania drivers to choose whether to present their vehicle registration in paper or electronic form.
Under the legislation, drivers who choose to present an electronic registration on a mobile device would retain control of their device. Police officers could only review the registration, would be required to promptly return the device after verification and could not use presentation of the electronic registration as consent to access other data or applications on the phone.
“Safer roads start with giving local law enforcement the right tools to do their jobs. With modern RADAR technology, our officers will have the precision and efficiency they need to enforce speed limits and help keep our families and communities safe,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “We took steps to modernize how we verify vehicle registration while also giving municipalities another tool to make our roads safer. I’m proud to see these priorities advance out of committee and continue working to modernize and add convenience to Pennsylvania’s transportation policies.”
Miller’s initiative to modernize electronic vehicle registration is informed by discussions with constituents during his Coffee & Conversation events, as well as by direct input from local police departments across his district regarding the need for enhanced tools to support community safety.

Senate Democratic Policy Committee Hearing on Addressing Today’s Challenges in Agriculture and Farming
October 6, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA − October 6, 2026 −
Senate Democratic Policy Committee Chair Nick Miller (D-14) hosted a policy hearing on addressing today’s challenges in agriculture and farming, alongside co-hosts Senator Judy Schwank (D-11) and Senator James Malone (D-36). This hearing examined current state-level tools and supports while identifying forward‑looking policy solutions. As stakeholders face challenges like workforce impacts, disease management, severe weather, and rising input costs, the Committee heard expert testimony from Secretary Redding and other industry leaders.
“Pennsylvania farmers are facing growing challenges, from rising costs and unpredictable weather to a shrinking pipeline of young farmers,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “We must act now to ensure agriculture remains a cornerstone of our Commonwealth. Today’s hearing highlighted important solutions we can consider to provide farmers with the resources they need, support the next generation, and protect Pennsylvania’s agricultural heritage.”
“Today’s hearing was a valuable opportunity to get an understand of what this past year has looked like for Pennsylvania agriculture,” said
Senator Judy Schwank
. “Every single one of us depends on our farmers and our agriculture sector provide us with the foods and products we need to go about our daily lives. Hearing from farmers and our Secretary Redding about Pennsylvania’s agricultural landscape is always valuable.”
“As someone who grew up farming, supporting the farmers and ag businesses I represent in Lancaster is a top priority for me,” said
Senator James Andrew Malone
. “Today, we heard from a farm operator in my district, Duane Swanger, that the rising cost of fuel, fertilizer, and seed are some of the biggest challenges our farmers are facing right now. We also heard that low-interest loan opportunities for farmers and support for addressing challenges like the avian influenza have been critical for his family’s farm. I look forward to continuing these critical programs and exploring new ways we can support farmers as they do the important work of feeding our state and nation.”
Secretary Russell Redding, Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture, testified on the state of the agricultural economy and its impact on our farmers and food system.
“Swirling around harvest and fall activities, every farmer is doing math right now, and this year the numbers are harder than they should be,” said Secretary Redding. “While no year is without challenges, the convergence of factors, such as climate disasters, rising prices on critical supplies such as diesel, geopolitical events, federal policy shifts, and market changes over the past several years have created a tremendously difficult farm economy, which has impacts on the foundations of our food system. But here is what farming has taught me: every time we plant a seed, we are making a bet on a strong harvest and a better tomorrow. In that spirit, today’s conversation is a seed – what we plant here, together, is how we make sure that tomorrow is better for Pennsylvania’s farmers, producers, and families who are counting on us.”
Noah Erwin, the Associate Director for Policy at Pasa Sustainable Agriculture, emphasized the need to help farmers maintain viable businesses and work environments.
“First, making important changes to our farmland preservation program would go a long way in helping to keep farmers farming,” said Erwin. “USDA’s 2022 Census of Agriculture showed that Pennsylvania leads the nation in the percentage of farmers under 35. We should be proud of that and continue to invest in programs that encourage young folks to farm. If we want to keep these folks in farming, however, we must do more to help make long-term land access and security a reality. Buying, or even leasing, land has become all but impossible in some places. An off-farm job for at least one, if not both, adults in the household is necessary to have the cash flow for affording land.”
Erwin also testified that Pennsylvania should also join the 16 other states who allow all workers to apply for a driver’s license.
“Currently, half of workers hired in agriculture do not have immigration status or work permits,” said Erwin. “Providing driver’s license access to all workers in agriculture and food sectors supports farm businesses and our food system and also makes our roads safer. House Bill 1518 is one of the proposals out there, though it has also not received a vote.”
Matt Espenshade, the President of the Pennsylvania State Grange and a seventh-generation dairy farmer from Lancaster County spoke on the future of agriculture.
“For our family, the future of agriculture is not an abstract policy discussion. It is the question of whether the next generation will have a fair opportunity to farm,” said Espenshade. “Pennsylvania agriculture supports more than 48,800 farms, contributes approximately $132.5 billion to the Commonwealth’s economy and supports nearly 600,000 jobs. Those numbers demonstrate agriculture’s strength, but they can hide how financially fragile many individual farms remain. Farmers face volatile commodity prices, severe weather, animal disease, workforce shortages and sharply higher costs for fertilizer, fuel, electricity, feed, equipment and repairs.”
In addition, Espenshade highlighted the impact of Chobani’s decision to invest $1.2 billion in a Pennsylvania facility, a move regarded as one of the most significant opportunities the dairy industry has seen in a generation.
“The project is expected to create more than 900 jobs and, at full scale, source more than three billion pounds of Pennsylvania milk each year – approximately 30 percent of the milk currently produced in the Commonwealth,” said Espenshade. “Production is expected to begin in 2027. That new demand is tremendously encouraging, but milk production cannot be expanded with the flip of a switch. Growing a herd requires cows, feed, land, barns, manure storage, financing, permits and trained workers. Farmers will need dependable market signals and sufficient time to make responsible decisions. Public policy should help farms grow carefully and profitably, not pressure them into expansion without secure contracts or sound business plans.”

Yaw, Miller Bill Limiting Use of PFAS in Firefighting Foam Approved by Senate
October 5, 2026
HARRISBURG
–
October 5, 2026
− A bill to limit the use of firefighting foam containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was approved by the state Senate today, according to Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) and Sen. Nick Miller (D-14), sponsors of the measure.
Senate Bill 980
would restrict the manufacture, sale, distribution and use of firefighting foam containing PFAS beginning in 2027. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, PFAS are man-made chemicals used since the 1940s that can accumulate in the environment and the human body over time, with studies linking exposure to adverse health effects.
“Compared to other emergency responders, firefighters can face significantly higher levels of PFAS exposure, putting them on the front lines of this national public health challenge,” Yaw said. “This bill is a commonsense response which has already been adopted by many states. It will undoubtedly protect firefighters moving forward, while also safeguarding our ground and surface water from contamination.”
“This bipartisan legislation takes decisive action to phase out dangerous substances, protecting the long-term health of our frontline heroes while preventing lasting contamination of our soil and water,” said Miller. “It reflects our responsibility to those who risk their lives in service to our communities. I look forward to advancing this bill as we put the well-being of those who serve at the forefront, safeguard public health and advocate for environmental protection.”
The lawmakers said the bill reflects years of collaboration with fire service leaders, emergency responders and industry representatives since its introduction in 2019. The proposal would allow fire companies to use Fire Company and Emergency Medical Services Grant funding to cover the cost of properly disposing of PFAS-containing foam. The state fire commissioner, working with the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, would oversee safe and environmentally responsible disposal.
The bill includes an exemption for facilities where PFAS-based foam remains necessary for safety, such as airports, chemical plants, oil refineries and sites handling flammable liquids or natural gas.
Senate Bill 980 now moves to the House of Representatives for consideration.

.

Senate Democratic Policy Committee Hearing on Micromobility Solutions & Safety
September 1, 2026
ALLENTOWN, PA − September 1, 2026 −
Senate Democratic Policy Committee Chair Nick Miller (D-14) held a policy hearing on micromobility solutions and safety, alongside co-host Senator Tim Kearney (D-26). This hearing examined steps the General Assembly could take toward meaningful safety and age rules for privately owned e-scooters, and how such micromobility issues intersect with infrastructure and public policy. It will also explore Abby’s Law (SB
1008
of 2025-26).
“With the recent increase in deaths and serious injuries involving motorcycles, e-bikes and other micromobility devices, we need to make sure our laws and infrastructure are keeping pace with how people are traveling,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “E-bikes and e-scooters can help connect people to jobs, close transportation gaps and provide more affordable ways to get around, but safety has to come first. This hearing is about bringing together law enforcement, transportation advocates and other stakeholders to identify common-sense rules that protect riders, pedestrians and drivers while allowing these transportation options to continue growing responsibly.”
“Abby’s Law is a bipartisan, commonsense bill named after Abby Gillon who tragically lost her young life at 12 while riding an e-scooter with her friend, Bella. The Senate shouldn’t let another year go by without action,” said
Senator Tim Kearney
, the bill’s sponsor, who introduced SB1008. “Today’s testimony underscored why this legislation is needed and why Republican leadership in the Senate must stop stalling. Public safety shouldn’t sit in committee —it should be a shared priority for all of us.”
Becky Bradley, Executive Director of Lehigh Valley Planning Commission, opened the hearing with a framework for micro-mobility and protected bike lanes in the Commonwealth.
“Investing in protected bike lanes and micro-mobility is about creating streets where people feel safe and comfortable with choosing these modes as viable and efficient transportation options,” said Bradley. “By supporting these bills, the General Assembly of Pennsylvania would be contributing to thoughtful short-term actions and coordinated long-term planning, from which your communities can build networks and infrastructure that is safer, more equitable, more resilient and more economically successful now and into the future.”
Henry Beaver, Special Assistant to the Deputy Secretary for Multimodal Transportation, spoke on the critical considerations for micromobility devices.
“PennDOT agrees that the Commonwealth needs statewide legal frameworks for both low-speed e-scooters and micromobility devices more broadly that acknowledge the widespread proliferation of micromobility devices while providing the necessary safeguards to protect users,” said Beaver. “In general, low-speed e-scooters should be regulated much the same as pedalcycles, and core rules and requirements should apply equally to private and commercial use of low-speed e-scooters.”
Scott Slingerland, Executive Director of the Coalition for Appropriate Transportation (CAT), testified about the importance of gathering data on bicycle crashes and how state legislators can use this information to make informed decisions.
“CAT has been seeking our two largest hospital networks (St. Luke’s Health Network and Lehigh Valley-Jefferson) to aggregate their Emergency Room admission data,” said Slingerland. “Knowing that most bicycle crashes are solo falls (League of American Bicyclists and CyclingSavvy) and are not reported to the police, hospital data would be very helpful for determining trends.”
Samantha Pearson, Healthy Communities Program Manager, and Ngani Ndimbie, Director of Programs at Mobilify Southwestern Pennsylvania, outlined the key points from their testimony.
“Micromobility devices are expanding access and mobility for Pennsylvanians who rely on them. There is a clear need to improve safety outcomes and to better define how these devices should be integrated into the broader transportation system.”
Chief Charles Roca of the Allentown Police Department discussed the local impact of micromobility use and related fatalities.
“When it’s on the road, it’s not a toy, it’s a form of conveyance,” Roca said. “In Allentown, we work closely with our partners in violence prevention. One life lost is one too many. When we experience a fatality involving someone using micromobility, it affects not only that individual, but also their family and the community.”
Chief Donald Sabo of the Salisbury Township Police Department emphasized how this is an issue affecting all regions.
“This is not just an urban environment issue, it transcends boroughs, townships, and cities throughout the Commonwealth,” said Sabo.
Scott L. Bohn, Executive Director of Pennsylvania Chiefs of Police Association, believes Pennsylvania must get safety right.
“Pennsylvania should not settle for partial regulation. At a minimum, legislation should require a uniform statewide framework,” said Bohn.

title: Lehigh Valley’s Tallest Mural Completed at Allentown’s Iconic Spiral Deck

Lehigh Valley’s Tallest Mural Completed at Allentown’s Iconic Spiral Deck
August 19, 2026
Artists Michael Rice and Brian Wentworth transform downtown landmark with monumental public artwork honoring Allentown’s silk industry, women’s labor and the city’s evolving future
ALLENTOWN, PA − August 19, 2026
−
Allentown Mural Arts and the Lehigh Valley Arts & Cultural Alliance (LVACA), in partnership with the Allentown Parking Authority, State Senator Nick Miller, Community Action Development Allentown, Allentown Economic Development Corporation, DLP Capital and the Allentown Arts Commission, are pleased to announce the completion of a monumental new public mural on the south façade of Allentown’s iconic Spiral Deck parking garage at 8th and Linden Streets.
Rising 135 feet above downtown,
“Penelope’s Echo—Threads of Tomorrow” is the tallest mural in the Lehigh Valley
, transforming one of Allentown’s most recognizable structures into a powerful new landmark celebrating the city’s history, creativity and future.
The project was made possible through grants and support secured by Senator Nick Miller’s office, Community Action Development Allentown, the Allentown Arts Commission and private funding from DLP Capital. The Renaissance Allentown Hotel and City Center Group also supported the project.
Selected through a competitive Request for Qualifications process, nationally renowned artists
Michael Rice and Brian Wentworth
created the original mural to reflect the history, innovation and creativity shaping Allentown’s rapidly evolving Downtown West neighborhood. Installation began April 17 and was completed in two phases, culminating in August.
Built in 1969, the eight-story Spiral Deck is a defining architectural feature of downtown Allentown. A façade that once faced a quiet alley now overlooks a vibrant corridor transformed by major new destinations, including the Da Vinci Science Center, new residential developments, Moxy Downtown Allentown and Archer Music Hall. The mural creates a highly visible cultural landmark within this emerging neighborhood and reflects the energy of Allentown’s ongoing revitalization.
Rice’s design,
“Penelope’s Echo—Threads of Tomorrow,”
draws inspiration from Allentown’s rich industrial past, particularly its silk and textile industry and the thousands of women whose labor powered it. The mural features Penelope, the mythological figure associated with weaving, patience and perseverance, alongside imagery inspired by a loom and flowing threads. Together, these elements connect the city’s industrial heritage with themes of creativity, resilience and innovation.
“I was inspired while researching the history of Allentown’s silk industry when I learned that women historically made up the majority of the workforce in the mills and how they played a prominent role in pushing women’s rights into the national conversation,” said
Michael Rice
.
At its height, Allentown was one of the nation’s most important silk manufacturing centers. By bringing the largely untold story of its women workers into the contemporary cityscape, the mural honors generations of women whose skill, labor and perseverance helped shape Allentown while creating a visual connection between the city’s past and its future.
“The installation of this new mural on Allentown’s Spiral Deck represents a significant transformation, adding vibrancy to an underutilized space that will add to the experience of visitors in downtown Allentown,” said
State Senator Nick Miller
. “Public art in other areas of the city has turned ordinary spaces into thriving art destinations, showcasing our region’s rich history and culture. This mural will showcase our region’s deep industrial history, spotlighting the perseverance of silk and garment workers. I’m proud to have secured part of the funding to bring this vision to life and to invest in public art that supports local creativity and strengthens our shared spaces.”
Pennsylvania’s third-largest city, Allentown has experienced significant growth and transformation over the past two decades, including more than $1 billion in downtown investment and approximately two million square feet of new commercial and residential development. Public art has become an important part of that transformation, bringing history, culture and creativity into the public realm while strengthening neighborhood identity and creating memorable experiences for residents and visitors.
The Spiral Deck mural is part of Allentown’s broader, multi-year public art initiative to integrate art into everyday life, celebrate the city’s diverse history and culture, foster neighborhood pride and create welcoming and inspiring public spaces.

title: Senate Democratic Policy Committee Members Investigate Strategies for Lowering Consumer Grocery Costs

Senate Democratic Policy Committee Members Investigate Strategies for Lowering Consumer Grocery Costs
July 31, 2026
PITTSBURGH, PA − July 31, 2026 −
Senate Democratic Policy Committee Chair Nick Miller (D-14) held a policy hearing on lowering consumer grocery costs, alongside co-host Senate Democratic Leader Senator Costa (D-43). This hearing examined the status of grocery affordability for Pennsylvanians and food production-related pressures including rising input costs (such as fuel, fertilizer), cost of climate impacts, and safeguarding from pathogens or other hazards.
“Every week I hear from families across my district that every trip to the grocery store is putting more strain on their pockets, while our farmers are facing growing challenges from unpredictable weather, rising production costs, and other pressures beyond their control,” said
Senator Miller
. “As Chair of the Senate Democratic Policy Committee, I convened this hearing to better understand what’s driving these costs and identify practical solutions to help develop policies that strengthen Pennsylvania agriculture, protect our food supply, and help make groceries more affordable for working families.”
“Senate Democrats have been laser focused on delivering real affordability for Pennsylvania’s families, ensuring that costs stay down while pay goes up,” said
Senate Democratic leader Senator Costa
. “Today’s hearing provided incredible insights into the myriad factors driving up costs at the grocery stores and making it hard for families to make ends meet. I look forward to taking today’s feedback to Harrisburg so that we can continue the work of improving the lives of every Pennsylvanian.”
Wendell Young IV, President of UFCW Local 1776
, representing nearly 30,000 workers across about 100 contracts, explained how tariffs are harming members firsthand. The Trump tariffs have led to plant closures, job losses, reduced hours, wage stagnation, and hiring freezes. At JBS Souderton, a major beef processing plant set to close on August 14th where they represent 1,400 members, increased transportation costs, inconsistent federal trade policies, and chaotic immigration policies have created severe uncertainty for hundreds of workers. Similarly, at Post Consumer Brands’ pet food facility in Bloomsburg, PA, more than 100 members in wet food production were laid off due to rising can costs driven by federal tariff policies.
“Consumers will feel this price impact immediately, workers will be left in the dust, and taxpayers will shoulder the burden with increased public assistance costs,”
said Young
. “In conclusion, this is the story that needs to be told about how our federal government is creating chaos and increasing costs for working families in Pennsylvania and our country.”
In written testimony, the Pennsylvania Food Merchants Association emphasized that rising costs of living are stretching family budgets across the state, and that the affordability of everyday essentials, especially food, remains a major concern for Pennsylvania residents.
Pennsylvania Secretary of Agriculture Russell Redding
emphasized in his written testimony that farmers are facing unprecedented pressures from rising production costs, labor shortages, unpredictable weather, and emerging plant and animal diseases. Additionally, global supply chain disruptions, international conflicts, tariffs, and market consolidation have contributed to higher grocery prices for Pennsylvania’s consumers. Despite strong state investments and efforts to build a resilient food system, many producers operate with narrowing margins and have limited control over commodity prices, while elevated costs for fertilizer, feed, fuel, and equipment continue to strain farm viability.
“Affordability doesn’t begin in the checkout lane. It begins with building food systems that are resilient competitive and work for everyone,”
said Secretary Redding.
“That means recognizing a simple truth: we cannot have affordable food without successful farms. We cannot have food security without resilient supply chains. We can’t build a stronger Commonwealth unless everyone, from the producer to the consumer, has a place at the table.”
Representing the charitable food network, Julie Bancroft of Feeding Pennsylvania, Colleen Young of the Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank, and Jordan Golin of Jewish Family and Community Services of Pittsburgh drew attention to the increased traffic to food banks, even as the costs of purchasing and transporting food has gone up for the charitable food systems. Between increased operational costs and increased needs, charitable food networks are doing more with less to address food insecurity across Pennsylvania.
“Transportation costs add another layer,”
said Julie Bancroft.
“The mid-Atlantic regional cooperative feeding PA program that supplies produce to thirty seven food banks in 14 states along the eastern seaboard has seen delivery costs rise sharply. The cost to ship a truckload of produce from Philadelphia to the Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank – last year that was $1475. That same truck of produce now costs $1775 to get across the state. Also, the average cost per pound of produce has increased from 22 cents to thirty cents. All of this leaves food banks scrambling to do more with less, just as families are doing the same.”
“Our neighborhood food pantry – our costs are going up by about $100,000 a year,”
said Jordan Golin.
“Why is that happening?…Rising food costs, food inflation, cuts to government support for food banks across the country, and we’re seeing the increased need of families across our region coming to us. So the numbers of people we’re serving are going up as the cost of food is also going up, and the resources to provide this food are going down.”
Testifiers for the hearing included:
Russell Redding, Pennsylvania Secretary of Agriculture
Wendell Young, United Food & Commercial Workers Local #1776
Julie Bancroft, Feeding Pennsylvania
Colleen Young, Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank
Jordan Golin, Jewish Family and Community Services (JFCS) of Pittsburgh
Senator Nick Miller was elected Policy Chair of the Senate Democratic Caucus in December 2024.

state

Senator Miller Applauds 2026-27 State Budget Investments in Education, Community Safety, and Relief for Pennsylvanians
July 12, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA – July 12, 2026 –
Senator Miller (D-Lehigh/Northampton) releases the following statement on today’s passage of the state budget:
“Today, we passed a fiscally responsible $50.8 billion budget that puts Pennsylvania families first,” said
Senator Miller
. “This budget makes historic investments in public education, strengthens community safety, supports family sustaining jobs, and delivers meaningful relief for working families. From improving local roads and bridges to supporting small businesses, expanding violence prevention programs, and providing more than $200 million in tax relief, these investments will make a real difference for families in the Lehigh Valley and across the Commonwealth.”
Investing in Public Education
As a former member of the 2023 Basic Education Funding Commission (BEFC), Senator Miller helped develop the bipartisan adequacy funding formula that continues to guide Pennsylvania’s historic investment in public education.
This year’s budget provides $565 million through the bipartisan adequacy formula, along with $154 million for Career and Technical Education, $125 million for school facility improvements, $100 million for school safety and school-based mental health supports, $330 million for Pre-K Counts, and $91.9 million for Head Start.
These investments advance Pennsylvania’s constitutional obligation to adequately fund public education while strengthening early learning, career readiness, student well-being, and safe learning environments.
“Every child deserves access to a high-quality education, regardless of their ZIP code,” said Senator Miller. “This budget builds on the bipartisan work to fairly fund our schools while investing in safer classrooms, stronger career and technical education, early childhood learning, and student mental health. These investments create more opportunity for students today and a stronger Pennsylvania for generations to come.”
Relief for Working Families & Retirees
The budget delivers more than $200 million in tax relief for Pennsylvanians under the Working Pennsylvanian Tax Credit, expanding the Child and Dependent Care Enhancement Tax Credit by increasing Pennsylvania’s match from 30% to 100% of the federal credit and raising the maximum benefit from $630 to $2,100 per family, and establishing an Employer Child Care Contribution Tax Credit to help businesses offset employees’ childcare costs.
“Working families deserve a tax system that helps them get ahead, not just get by,” said Senator Miller. “These tax credits will put more money back into the pockets of hardworking Pennsylvanians, make childcare more affordable, and help parents stay in the workforce.”
In addition, there will be much needed relief through a long‑overdue cost‑of‑living adjustment for retired teachers, police officers, and firefighters who left service before July 2, 2001. This adjustment would finally provide a COLA to more than 40,000 retired educators and support professionals who have not received a pension increase since 2002.
Supporting Child Care Workers
The budget invests $30 million in childcare worker retention bonuses, a $5 million increase over last year, to help recruit and retain the workforce families depend on. The funding is expected to provide bonuses of approximately $540 to more than 55,000 childcare workers across Pennsylvania, helping strengthen the childcare system and support working parents.
“When we invest in the professionals who care for our children, we make it possible for parents to stay in the workforce and provide for their families,” said Senator Miller. “This simply allows our working parents to work and have our childcare workers have additional support that they need. These retention bonuses recognize the essential role childcare workers play every day while helping providers recruit and retain the dedicated educators our communities depend on.”
Delivering on Family-Sustaining Jobs
The budget makes strategic investments to strengthen Pennsylvania’s economy, including $775 million for local roads and bridges, $125 million for Innovate in PA 2.0 to accelerate entrepreneurship and life sciences innovation, and $23.7 million to support historically disadvantaged businesses, a $3.75 million increase over last year. These investments will improve infrastructure, expand access to capital, and create opportunities for businesses and workers across the Commonwealth.
“Pennsylvania’s future depends on smart investments that create jobs, support entrepreneurs, and improves the infrastructure our communities rely on,” said Senator Miller. “This investment strengthens our workforce, grows our economy, and positions Pennsylvania to compete for the industries of tomorrow.”
Preventing EBT Card Theft
The budget includes $7 million to implement chip-enabled EBT cards, strengthening protections against SNAP benefit theft. Unlike magnetic stripe cards, chip technology generates a unique code for each transaction, making it significantly harder for criminals to steal benefits through card skimming. Nationwide, an estimated 3.5 million SNAP recipients have been affected by benefit theft.
“Too many families in our communities have had their EBT benefits stolen, leaving them without the resources they rely on to put food on the table,” said Senator Miller. “No one should lose their grocery money to fraud. Investing in chip-enabled EBT cards is a commonsense step that protects vulnerable Pennsylvanians, strengthens the integrity of the SNAP program, and gives families greater peace of mind when they need it most.”
Supporting Student Teachers
The budget invests $40 million in student teacher stipends, a $10 million increase over last year, to help aspiring educators complete their full-time, unpaid student teaching requirement without facing unnecessary financial hardship.
The investment helps strengthen Pennsylvania’s educator pipeline by making it more affordable for future teachers to enter the profession.
“Pennsylvania’s future depends on the teachers we prepare today and the support we give them from the start,” said Senator Miller. “For too long, aspiring educators have been expected to work full-time in the classroom without pay, creating a financial barrier that discourages talented individuals from entering the profession.”
Strengthening Public Safety
The budget makes significant investments to improve public safety across Pennsylvania, including $62.15 million for violence intervention and prevention programs, $10 million for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program to help protect organizations against hate crimes, funding for four new Pennsylvania State Police cadet classes totaling 480 cadets, and increased maximum loan amounts for fire and EMS companies to strengthen emergency response capabilities.
“Strong public safety requires investing in prevention, preparedness, and the people who protect our communities every day,” said Senator Miller. “These investments will strengthen violence prevention programs, enhance security for organizations at-risk of hate crimes, support the recruitment of new State Police cadets, and provide firefighters and EMS companies with the resources they need to respond when Pennsylvanians need them most. This is a comprehensive investment in safer, stronger communities across our Commonwealth.”
Nursing Home Budget Adjustment (BAF)
Nursing Home Budget Adjustment Factor (BAF) will receive $81 million in additional funding for nursing homes, along with extending the Department of Human Services’ authority to use the Budget Adjustment Factor for two more years, provides much-needed stability for providers.
This investment builds on Senator Miller’s leadership as Senate Democratic Policy Chair, where he convened a policy hearing examining the long-term sustainability of Pennsylvania’s nursing homes, the state’s rapidly aging population and workforce shortages, and the urgent steps needed to ensure older adults continue to have access to quality long-term care.
“Pennsylvania’s nursing homes are facing significant financial pressures, and without action, access to quality long-term care for seniors is at risk,” said Senator Miller. “Nearly 70 percent of nursing home residents rely on Medicaid, making a sustainable reimbursement system essential to keeping these facilities open and delivering the care families depend on, while ensuring our seniors continue to receive the care and dignity they deserve.”
Additional Budget Investments
The budget also includes several key investments that will strengthen communities across Pennsylvania, including:
$2.5 million for the Nursing Shortage Assistance Program to help address Pennsylvania’s nursing workforce shortage.
$16.3 million for apprenticeship and workforce training programs through the Department of Labor & Industry.
$24.1 million for rape crisis centers.
$979 million for mental health services.
$42.5 million for Grow PA Scholarships to help recruit and retain students in high-demand fields.
In the coming weeks, Senator Miller will highlight how these investments will directly benefit the Lehigh Valley and the communities of the 14th Senatorial District.
“This budget invests in families, strengthens our workforce, improves public safety, and creates greater opportunity across Pennsylvania,” said Senator Miller. “While there is more work ahead, these investments move our Commonwealth in the right direction and will make a meaningful difference for communities throughout the Lehigh Valley and across Pennsylvania.”

Senator Nick Miller Urges Senate Republicans to Schedule Vote on Responsible Data Center Regulations to Protect Pennsylvanians
July 11, 2026
July 11, 2026
− As communities across Pennsylvania raise concerns about the rapid growth of data centers and their impact on energy costs, Senator Nick Miller is calling on Senate Republicans to bring bipartisan legislation to the Senate floor that protects ratepayers, strengthens local communities, and establishes clear statewide standards for responsible development.
“Pennsylvania needs strict, enforceable guardrails around data center development,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “These projects cannot come at the expense of higher utility bills, strained infrastructure, or communities being left out of the process even if it creates economic opportunities. Families should never be forced to subsidize the cost of powering billion-dollar tech corporations.”
Several bills addressing data center development recently passed the House of Representatives with bipartisan support. The bills have been referred to Senate Committees, where they await consideration.
House Bill 1834
would place strict, enforceable guardrails on data center developments, establishing the Commonwealth’s first statewide framework to protect ratepayers, prevent the costs of powering massive data centers from being passed on to hardworking families, require investments in clean energy and programs like LIHEAP for energy assistance, and ensure corporate growth doesn’t come at the expense of hardworking Pennsylvanians.
House Bill 2496
would allow local municipalities to implement a 6-month pause on data center developments to spend time updating their zoning ordinances.
House Bill 2650
, Governor Shapiro’s GRID Standards proposal, would establish strong, enforceable standards for data center developments to protect energy affordability, invest in local communities, and protect the environment.
At a time when families are already struggling to afford groceries, housing, and rising utility bills, the legislature cannot allow additional costs to fall on consumers. Responsible data center development can balance economic growth with affordability and accountability.
This effort builds on Senator Miller’s work as Senate Democratic Policy Chair to lower energy costs and advance strategies that protect Pennsylvania families from rising utility bills in June 2026. It also follows his Senate Democratic Caucus Policy Hearing on the impacts of data centers and the policy solutions needed to protect residential ratepayers while planning for the Commonwealth’s growing energy demands.
“It is time to put Pennsylvania residents first and advance responsible legislation that protects ratepayers, strengthens communities, and ensures our energy future works for everyone,” said Senator Miller.

title: Senator Nick Miller Announces $50,000 to Launch Restoration Planning for Allentown’s Historic West Park Bandshell

Senator Nick Miller Announces $50,000 to Launch Restoration Planning for Allentown’s Historic West Park Bandshell
June 30, 2026
ALLENTOWN, PA –
Senator Nick Miller announced that the
Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission (PHMC)
has awarded a $25,000 Keystone Historic Preservation Grant to the West Park Civic Association to support the initial planning phases for the preservation and restoration of West Park’s historic bandshell. Combined with the $25,000 Senator Miller secured in last year’s state budget for the project, the West Park Civic Association will receive a total of $50,000 to help preserve this historic community landmark.
Keystone Historic Preservation Grants help identify, preserve, promote, and protect Pennsylvania’s historic and archaeological resources while contributing to community revitalization efforts.
The grants are funded through the Keystone Recreation, Park & Conservation Fund, which receives annual support from a portion of the state’s realty transfer tax revenue.
“West Park has been a centerpiece of community life in Allentown for generations, bringing residents together through arts, culture, and public events,” said
Senator Miller
. “This investment will help preserve one of our city’s most treasured historic landmarks, ensuring the iconic 1907 bandshell continues to serve as a gathering place for future generations.”
“The West Park Civic Association is pleased to move forward with plans to restore the West Park bandshell, made possible in part by Senator Nick Miller’s support through the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources,” said
Thomas Yuracka, WPCA Board President
. “Dating to 1908 and designed by noted Philadelphia architect Horace Trumbauer, the West Park bandshell is the only remaining wooden bandshell of his design.”
The grant will support electrical, structural, and architectural assessments, as well as historic preservation planning and documentation necessary for the restoration of the bandshell. Designed in the Beaux-Arts style by renowned architect Horace Trumbauer, the 1907 bandshell remains a defining feature of West Park and an important venue for community and cultural programming.
The funding also enabled the association to consult with Richard Grubb and Associates on cultural resource services. This work included securing eligibility for West Park to be listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

title: Senate Democratic Policy Committee Hearing on Lowering Your Electric Bill

Senate Democratic Policy Committee Hearing on Lowering Your Electric Bill
June 23, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA − June 23, 2026 −
Senate Democratic Policy Committee Chair Nick Miller (D-14) hosted a policy hearing examining solutions to lower consumer electric bills, alongside Senator Kane and Senator Malone. Experts provided testimony regarding strategies to achieve cost-savings solutions for residential ratepayers in Pennsylvania.
“Electricity should be affordable, reliable, and available to every Pennsylvanian,” said
Senator Nick Miller
. “Families, seniors, and small businesses across our Commonwealth are facing growing pressure from rising energy costs, and they deserve action. Today’s hearing focused on identifying real-world solutions to increase energy supply, modernize our infrastructure, improve efficiency, and protect ratepayers. Pennsylvania has the resources and expertise to lead on energy policy, and our goal must be simple: lower costs, strengthen reliability, and put consumers first.”
“Pennsylvanians work hard for their money, and they deserve to know they’re getting a fair deal when it comes to their electric bills,” said
Senator John Kane
. “This hearing is about finding real, common-sense solutions to lower energy costs and protect consumers from unfair and exploitative practices. As legislators, it’s our responsibility to make sure the rules work for the people, not against them, and to ensure every Pennsylvanian is protected from deceptive business practices.”
“The reality is PPL Electric, the electric provider in our region, has seen a steadily growing profit margin since 2019,” said
Senator James Malone
. “I think we need to be asking hard questions about why they are consistently asking for rate increases when they have the ability to invest back into their systems and spare ratepayers. I was pleased to join today’s hearing with my colleagues to ask these questions and explore ways we can lower electric bills for families in Lancaster and across Pennsylvania.”
Vice-Chair Kim Barrow, Commissioner of Pennsylvania PUC, testified on the position electricity customers are facing today and the drastic changes in the energy landscape with the influx of new demand.
“Rising electricity bills are a national issue with the average residential customer price jumping 10.2% to 18.8 cents/kWh in March from 17.1 cents/kWh a year earlier,” said Barrow. “The supply portion of the electric bill is being driven by many factors: slow interconnection of new generation, retirement of baseload generation, increasing high voltage transmission builds, and the last three PJM capacity auctions which cleared 22% higher year over year for 3 years. Those capacity prices rose due to data center demand in PJM which is forecast to reach 32 GW by 2030.”
Alex Charlton, RESA State Chair for Government Relations at Constellation, stated that additional steps should be taken to ensure the Commonwealth remains a leader in both consumer protection and market innovation.
“We recognize that the competitive energy market is not perfect, just like other markets in consumer goods and services are imperfect,” said Charlton. “Keeping bad actors out and welcoming good actors in will help ensure the retail market can deliver the proper consumer protections, innovation, economic benefits, and consumer value, to the citizens of Pennsylvania.”
Darryl Lawrence of the Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate emphasized that keeping electricity affordable is essential to consumers’ well‑being. Lawrence recommended adopting fair ratemaking practices, requiring explicit consumer consent before switching customers to variable rates, and implementing strong safeguards to ensure hyperscale data centers do not drive-up costs or disrupt service for existing customers.
“To honor these pledges and policy choices and to protect existing ratepayers from these costs and risks, within Pennsylvania there is existing statutory authority and responsibility placing obligations upon the Commission and the EDCs to act in a manner that respects a cooperative federalism framework and that protects reliable and affordable electricity service for existing ratepayers while also meeting the new extraordinary electricity demand of data centers,” said Lawrence.
Testifiers for the hearing included:
Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission
Pennsylvania Utility Law Project
Energy Association of PA
Office of Consumer Advocate
Constellation
Senator Nick Miller was elected Policy Chair of the Senate Democratic Caucus in December 2024.

. Photographs and downloadable videos are available upon request.

title: Senator Nick Miller Announces $891,000 DCNR Grants for Lehigh County Parks and Trails
raw_text:
Senator Nick Miller Announces $891,000 DCNR Grants for Lehigh County Parks and Trails
October 13, 2026
HARRISBURG, PA
–
October 13, 2026
− Senator Nick Miller (D-Lehigh/Northampton) announced that two Lehigh County projects in the 14th Senatorial District will receive a combined $891,000 in grants through the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources’ Community Conservation Partnerships Program.
The funding will support improvements to Boroline Park in Emmaus Borough and the development of the Jordan Creek Greenway in South Whitehall Township.
The awards include:
$391,000 to Emmaus Borough
through the Federal Land and Water Conservation Fund for the rehabilitation of Boroline Park, including parking and baseball field improvements, a natural play area, new playground equipment, ADA accessibility, landscaping and other site improvements.
$500,000 to South Whitehall Township
through the Keystone Community Program for the development of the Jordan Creek Greenway, including approximately one mile of trail from Lapp Road to N. Cedar Crest Boulevard, ADA accessibility, landscaping and other site improvements.
“Every community deserves parks and outdoor spaces that are safe, accessible and welcoming for everyone,”
Senator Miller
said. “These investments will give Lehigh County residents more opportunities to enjoy the outdoors, stay active and connect with their communities. I’m proud to support projects that strengthen our neighborhoods and improve quality of life for residents.”
The Community Conservation Partnerships Program Grants, managed by the DCNR Bureau of Recreation and Conservation (BRC), builds connections between Pennsylvanians and the outdoors by supporting recreational improvements, natural resource conservation, and community revitalization efforts.
For more information, visit Senator Nick Miller’s newsroom at
PASenatorMiller.com/newsroom
.
###
Contact: Gail Vivar, 201-870-2378

ai_summary.summary: The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources awarded $891,000 in grants to two Lehigh County municipalities: $391,000 to Emmaus Borough for Boroline Park improvements and $500,000 to South Whitehall Township for a new Jordan Creek Greenway trail segment. Senator Miller announced the grants, which were administered through existing state and federal conservation programs.

title: Applications Now Open: Senator Miller Announces FY 2026-27 Statewide Building Opportunities through Out-of-School Time (BOOST)
raw_text:
Applications Now Open: Senator Miller Announces FY 2026-27 Statewide Building Opportunities through Out-of-School Time (BOOST)
October 16, 2026
October 16, 2026
− Senator Nick Miller (D-Lehigh/Northampton) announced that applications are now open for the 2026-27 Building Opportunities Through Out-of-School Time (BOOST) initiative, which provides funding to support youth-serving programs that help keep young people safe, engaged, and on track for success.
The 2026-27 state budget includes $11.5 million for the BOOST initiative, which supports upstream prevention efforts for school-age at risk youth, including mentoring, afterschool programs, and other out-of-school-time activities. Senator Nick Miller was appointed to the School Safety and Security Committee of the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency (PCCD), underscoring his commitment to public safety and the well-being of Pennsylvania’s students, educators, and residents.
“Every young person deserves access to safe, supportive environments and opportunities to reach their full potential, both inside and outside the classroom,” said
Senator Miller
. “Investing in afterschool and summer programs gives students access to positive role models, meaningful activities, and the support they need to succeed. These investments are critical to strengthening our communities, preventing youth violence, and ensuring Pennsylvania’s young people have the opportunity to build a brighter future.”
Eligibility and Application Deadline
This funding opportunity is open exclusively to statewide youth-serving nonprofit organizations with 501(c)(4) status. Applications must be submitted electronically through the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency’s (PCCD) Egrants system by 11:59 p.m. on Thursday, December 10, 2026.
Allowable Uses of Funding
BOOST grant funding may support direct program activities and related expenses, including:
Salaries and benefits for full-time and part-time personnel, including overtime
Contractor and consultant services
Supplies and equipment
Travel and training
Technical assistance
Referrals to community-based service providers and programs, including associated meals, incentives, and stipends
Other necessary program expenses, including grant management and capacity-building costs
The BOOST initiative is designed to strengthen prevention efforts and expand opportunities for young people through programs that promote positive development, connection, and community support.
For more information about the School Safety and Security Committee and its initiatives, visit the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency website at
www.pccd.pa.gov
.
###

ai_summary.summary: Senator Miller announced that applications are open for the state's BOOST program, which distributes $11.5 million in grants to statewide nonprofit organizations running afterschool and out-of-school youth programs. The funding comes from the FY 2026-27 state budget and is administered by the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency. Applications are due December 10, 2026, and are limited to statewide 501(c)(4) nonprofits.
